title: Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi
summary: The Kasubi Tombs stand on a hill in Kampala, Uganda. UNESCO says the former palace of the Kabakas of Buganda was built in 1882 and became a royal burial ground in 1884. Its circular, domed main building, the Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, holds four royal tombs and was built of wood, thatch, reeds and wattle. A fire later destroyed that building. UNESCO calls the site the most active religious place in the kingdom.

uncertainty.note: UNESCO: palace built in 1882, converted to a royal burial ground in 1884. The span runs from construction to conversion; the tombs remain in use.

as_recorded.value: built in 1882 and converted into the royal burial ground in 1884

importance.justification: UNESCO calls it the major spiritual centre for the Baganda and the burial ground of four Kabakas.

reviewer_note: No model: no height was found on a page I could open (Britannica, Met Museum and CyArk pages were blocked). The EBSCO page (Buganda entry) calls the site the graves of four kabakas at "Nabulagala, popularly known as the Kasubi Tombs"; it supports only the four-kabaka count. UNESCO describes the fire only as a "recent fire tragedy" without a year on the page, so the summary gives no year. UNESCO also says a tomb building has existed here since the 13th century; this record covers the 1882 palace and 1884 conversion.
